1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6.name: King's Indian Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6.background: Until the mid-1930s it was generally regarded as highly suspect, but the analysis and play of Alexander Konstantinopolsky, Isaac Boleslavsky and David Bronstein helped to make it much more respected and popular. It has been a favourite of the former world champions Garry Kasparov, Bobby Fischer and Mikhail Tal.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3.name: King's Indian Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3.strategy: The principal move: it develops a knight and prepares e4, the broad pawn centre that Black's set-up invites. White commits to space; Black commits to undermining that centre from a distance with pieces and pawn breaks instead of occupying it. This is where the opening's main battle is fought.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight towards the centre and keeps White flexible: a big pawn centre, a fianchetto or a quiet set-up all stay possible. It gives up the aggressive set-ups built on f3 or f4. The fianchetto plan that often follows is one of the most popular at grandmaster level.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3.name: King's Indian Defence: Fianchetto Variation, Immediate Fianchetto
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop at once: it watches the long diagonal and the centre and the king is safe behind it, but White gives up the idea of a broad pawn centre. The game turns quieter and more strategic, and with no knight on c3 yet Black may challenge the centre straight away.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3.name: Indian Defence: Anti-Grünfeld, Alekhine Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3.strategy: Prepares a broad pawn centre with e4, backed by a pawn instead of a knight. The price is high: the king's knight loses its natural square, the e1-h4 diagonal opens, and White usually has to castle on the queenside and attack on the kingside, while Black gets a lead in development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.d5.name: Indian Defence: Anti-Grünfeld, Advance Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.d5.strategy: Takes space and closes the centre, and rules out ...d5 for Black. But White commits the d-pawn before any piece is out and creates a target: Black will undermine it with pawn breaks on the queenside, and the pawn needs support. A playable way to avoid the main theory.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.h4.name: Indian Defence: Anti-Grünfeld, Basman-Williams Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.h4.background: First reached by Michael Basman in 1980, by the move order 1.c4 g6 2.h4 Nf6 3.d4, and taken up by Simon Williams in the 2000s; Williams himself prefers to call it the Harry Attack.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.h4.strategy: A surprise flank thrust that ignores development: the pawn aims for h5 to open lines against Black's kingside and ties the f6 knight to the defence of h5. The price is a pawn move before any piece is out and weak squares on g3 and g4 behind it. Black can simply develop.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Qc2.name: Queen's Pawn, Mengarini Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Qc2.strategy: Protects the c4 pawn from the start and prepares e4, but brings the queen out early without gaining anything by it. Black develops freely and keeps the choice between challenging the centre at once and waiting for White to build it. Harmless rather than ambitious.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.d5 b5.name: Indian Defence: Anti-Grünfeld, Adorjan Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.d5 b5.strategy: A pawn offer on the spot: if White takes, the b- and c-files open for Black's pieces and the queenside structure is shattered, in return for the pawn. A sharp, prepared sideline that uses the closed centre; if Black cannot show enough activity, White simply keeps the extra pawn and the space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.d5 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and does not react to the advanced pawn: the bishop's long diagonal points at White's queenside, and Black keeps every plan against the d5 pawn open. White has taken space and must now show what it is worth, while Black's position stays sound.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.d5 c6.strategy: Challenges the advanced pawn at once. If White supports it, Black keeps pressure on the pawn and on the c-file; if it is exchanged, Black's pieces get open lines at no cost in structure. A direct way to ask what the advance is really for.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.d5 d6.strategy: Holds e5 and prepares to develop in peace, but does nothing about the pawn on d5. White is left free to build the centre and the queenside space undisturbed, and Black is only reacting. Sound, yet not the most demanding reply.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 d5.name: Neo-Grünfeld Defence: Goglidze Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 d5.strategy: Challenges the centre at once. If White takes and builds the big centre, the black knight has to retreat, but White has lost time on f3 and the kingside lags behind; Black counters with pressure on the centre. The reply that fights for the centre most directly.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 c5.strategy: Strikes at the d4 pawn at once, while White has spent a move on f3. If White pushes the pawn to d5, Black gets a pawn structure with play on the queenside, and White a space edge but a kingside whose development f3 slows down. A flexible reply with a clear plan.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 e5.name: Indian Defence: Anti-Grünfeld, Alekhine Variation, Leko Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 e5.strategy: A gambit: after dxe5 the knight heads for h5, threatening ...Qh4+ down the diagonal that f3 has opened. White can parry that simply and keeps the extra pawn, so Black gets quick play against the kingside and little else for the pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 c5 4.d5.strategy: Gains space and fixes the pawn structure, escaping the pressure on d4. White gets a free hand in the centre; Black gets targets, since the d5 pawn can be attacked and the queenside is open for pawn play. The slow f3 pawn will matter if the position opens.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 c5 4.dxc5.strategy: Wins a pawn only for a moment: ...Qa5+ regains it at once, and Black gets the long diagonal and a lead in development against a White set-up already weakened by f3. White gives up the pawn centre for little.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 c5 4.e4.strategy: Builds the full centre at once, but the pawn on d4 is attacked and only the queen can recapture after ...cxd4. The queen is then hit by ...Nc6 and White loses time while Black develops easily.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 c5 4.d5 d6.strategy: Builds a solid pawn chain and takes e5 under control. Black accepts White's space and counts on queenside pawn play and pressure against the d5 pawn, and the pawn on d6 also gives the dark-squared bishop a solid pawn chain to work behind.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 c5 4.d5 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto before deciding how to meet White's space: the bishop takes the long diagonal and no pawn is committed yet, so Black can still build a solid chain or strike at the d5 pawn once White shows a set-up. The slow f3 pawn gives Black targets later.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 c5 4.d5 e6.strategy: Attacks the d5 pawn straight away, offering to trade Black's e-pawn for the pawn that cramps Black. Black gets a fluid structure and play against the centre, while White keeps space but has to keep d5 and e4 secure with a king's knight still short of a square.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 c5 4.d5 d6 5.e4.strategy: Completes the broad pawn centre that f3 was preparing, taking space and fixing the structure. The cost is development: f3 takes the natural square from the g1 knight, and Black will undermine the centre with pawn breaks while White looks for a kingside attack.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 c5 4.d5 d6 5.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and covers d5 and e4 before the pawn commits, so White keeps the choice of how to use the centre. The price is a slight delay in claiming the full pawn centre, which gives Black time to organise its breaks.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 c5 4.d5 d6 5.Bg5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, with an eye on the f6 knight. It does nothing for the centre White is aiming at, and Black can chase it at once with ...h6 and ...g5, so White spends time for little.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 c5 4.d5 d6 5.e4 Bg.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop is the base of Black's counterplay and the king can castle behind it. White has the space and the broad centre; Black keeps the structure flexible and waits for the moment to hit it, with pawn breaks on the queenside and against e4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 c5 4.d5 d6 5.e4 e6.strategy: Attacks the d5 pawn at once, offering to trade Black's e-pawn for White's spearhead. Black gets a fluid structure, with the c-pawn and the bishop free to work against the centre, while White keeps the space but has to look after d5 and e4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 c5 4.d5 d6 5.e4 Nb.strategy: Black's solid developing move protects c5 and e5. It commits to no pawn break and blocks the c8 bishop, so White keeps the initiative with its space and decides the character of the game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.f3 c5 4.d5 d6 5.e4 Bg.strategy: Develops the queenside knight to support e4 and d5, rounding off the chain of pawns on c4, d5 and e4. The king's knight still lacks a natural square because of f3, so White's development remains awkward. White has the space, Black the targets.

Finds a square for the king's knight, which f3 has taken away from its natural one: from e2 it supports the centre and can head for g3 or c3 as the position demands. White keeps the space and a solid structure and plays for the queenside.

Develops the bishop and prepares queenside castling, but the knights are still at home and f3 has taken the kingside knight's best square, so White's development is lopsided. Playable if White finds the time to catch up.

Attacks the d5 pawn with a pawn, offering to trade Black's e-pawn for White's space-gaining spearhead. Black gets a fluid structure with play against e4 and the queenside pawns ready to advance; White keeps the space but has to guard the central pawns.

Gets the king safe behind the fianchetto before the centre is resolved. White's centre only becomes dangerous once the pieces are placed, and f3 has already slowed the king's knight, so Black can pick the moment to strike with the pawn breaks it keeps in reserve.

Prepares ...b5 to attack the c4 pawn that holds d5 in place. The idea is useful but slow: the king is still in the centre and the pieces are undeveloped, so White gets time to complete its development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7.strategy: Matches White's fianchetto: the king's bishop belongs on the long diagonal anyway. Black stays flexible and keeps the choice between challenging the centre at once and letting White build it first.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d5.name: Neo-Grünfeld Defence: with g3
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d5.strategy: Challenges the centre at once with a pawn. White's fianchetto bishop will bear down on d5, and the centre is likely to be traded off; the game is a calm one in which White has no knight on c3 yet to meet the pawn directly.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d6.strategy: Takes the solid set-up in a different order: the pawn guards e5 and the bishop follows. Black cedes the centre for now and plans to attack it later, so it is sound but does nothing to disturb the quiet fianchetto.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop watches the long diagonal, fights for d5 and the queenside, and the king can castle behind it. White has not yet decided how to build the centre, which is the point of the quiet start.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight to its natural square, guarding d4 and e5, and keeps the choice of how to use the centre. White gets a quiet game with the king to be tucked away behind the fianchetto bishop, where Black's usual attacking plan has little to bite on.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Nc3.strategy: Brings the knight out to support e4 and d5, a sound but committal development: it takes the c3 square from the c-pawn, and Black can hit the centre at once with ...d5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and lines the bishop up against the d5 pawn: if Black ever lets the tension go, the bishop presses the centre and the queenside from the long diagonal. White accepts the tension on c4 and d5 and keeps the king safe.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight, guards d4 and e5 and leaves the tension on c4 and d5 as it is. Black is not forced to resolve the centre, and White's pieces are ready for a quiet game along the long diagonals once the bishop and castling are in.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d5 4.cxd5.strategy: Takes the pawn at once and gives up the pressure on d5. After ...Nxd5 the knight is active in the centre, and White must spend time challenging it. Playable, but it hands Black easy development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 Bg7.strategy: Develops the bishop behind the knight, so that after the central pawns are exchanged it bears down on d4. Both sides now have fianchettoed bishops, and the game becomes a manoeuvring fight over the centre rather than a race.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with a pawn, so that the long diagonal of the white bishop finds a solid target. The c8 bishop keeps its diagonal, and Black accepts a slightly passive set-up in exchange for a firm hold on the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn and opens the centre, but only for a moment: White regains it with the queen on a4 and c4 and is left with a free centre and a bishop aimed at the queenside. Black has traded away its central pawn for it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and lets White build the centre: the bishop is the base of Black's counterplay, and the king can castle safely behind it. Black accepts less space in exchange for a sound structure and a plan to attack the centre later.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5.strategy: Counterattacks before White has played e4. If White takes and builds the big centre, Black hits it with pieces and a break with the c-pawn; the play is sharper and more direct than with the quiet fianchetto. Black gets active pieces and an open game in return for giving White the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d6.strategy: Takes the solid set-up in the other order: the pawn guards e5 and the bishop follows. Black cedes the centre for the moment and plans to attack it later; the order barely matters unless White finds a set-up the late bishop does not meet.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.e4.strategy: Builds the full pawn centre that Black's set-up invites, with the knight on c3 to support it. White gets space and the initiative in the centre; Black gets targets and a long-term plan against the pawns. The sides then castle and attack on opposite wings, with unbalanced play.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight before committing the centre. White can still build the pawn centre with e4 later, but gives up the fast set-ups with f3 or f4. A more flexible and less committal approach than the immediate pawn advance.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.g3.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop instead of building the pawn centre at once. White controls the centre with pieces and keeps e4 for later, so the game is calmer and more manoeuvring, with the bishop pressing on the long diagonal.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 O-O.strategy: Castles at once and keeps the choice of set-up open: the king is safe, and Black decides between a King's Indian structure and a strike at the centre after seeing what White does.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 d6.strategy: Commits to the King's Indian set-up: the pawn controls e5 and prepares ...Nbd7 and ...e5. Black gives up the early ...d5 strike and lets White build the centre with e4, in return for a solid structure and a long game of manoeuvring.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 d5.strategy: Switches to the Grünfeld: Black strikes at the c4 pawn at once, because after White plays e4 the chance is gone. Black accepts a sharper game in which White's pawn centre becomes a target for the pieces rather than a strength.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 d6 5.g3.name: King's Indian Defence: Fianchetto Variation, Delayed Fianchetto
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 d6 5.g3.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop, which covers the king and eyes the centre. White gives up the broad e4 centre for a solid position and a slower, strategic game, with a kingside that Black's usual pawn storm hardly reaches.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 d6 5.Bg.name: King's Indian Defence: Smyslov Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 d6 5.Bg.strategy: Develops the bishop actively before the structure is settled and puts pressure on the f6 knight. It threatens nothing concrete: Black can drive the bishop back with ...h6 or ignore it, and White has placed the bishop before knowing where it belongs.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 d6 5.e4.strategy: Takes the full centre at once, the standard way to meet the King's Indian: the pawns on c4 and e4 claim space and the pieces develop behind them. White commits to a broad centre, and the game is about whether it proves a strength or a target for Black's pawn breaks.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 d6 5.g3.strategy: Castles and finishes the King's Indian set-up. Black keeps the central pawn breaks ready and has a safe king.

Develops the knight behind the e-pawn before castling, preparing the central break. The usual set-up arrives by a different order, though the knight blocks the c8 bishop, which is why castling first is the more direct path.

Develops against d4 and prepares the e-pawn break with a piece. The knight takes the c6 square from the c-pawn, and if White closes the centre with d5 it goes to the rim; playable, but it commits the knight before Black has seen White's set-up.

Completes the fianchetto: the bishop covers the king and eyes the centre from g2. White's kingside is more solid than in most King's Indian lines, so Black's normal plan of attack on that wing is hard to carry out.

Gains space at once and ends the tension on d4 before Black has challenged it with a pawn. White gets a cramping pawn and an easy fianchetto, but Black is left with clear queenside pawn breaks: playable, a fight between White's space and Black's counterplay.

Builds the broad pawn centre in the classical way while the king's bishop is still at home. The e4 pawn leans on the c3 knight, which ties it down, and Black strikes at the centre with a pawn break before the fianchetto is complete.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 O-O 5.g.strategy: Fianchettoes the bishop, which covers the king and eyes the centre. White gives up the e4 centre for a solid, flexible position; the kingside is so well covered that Black's usual attack has little to aim at.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 O-O 5.e.strategy: A compact set-up: the pawn supports d4 and opens the f1 bishop, with no ambition for a broad centre. The cost is that the c1 bishop is shut in and has to find another route, and White's play is slow and modest.

The classical way to meet the King's Indian: White takes space in the centre with the pawns on c4 and e4 and develops behind them. The big centre is both the asset and the risk, since Black will attack it with a pawn break and the game turns on whether it holds.
Black sets up the standard King's Indian formation. The pawn controls e5 and c5 and prepares to develop the b8 knight, while the fianchettoed bishop waits for the centre to open.
Strikes at the c4 pawn at once. Since White has chosen the modest e3, Black seizes the centre instead of waiting, the game opens, and White has to decide whether to take on d5 or defend the pawn.

Strikes at d4 from the side and opens the g7 bishop's diagonal. With the e3 pawn behind it d4 is firmly held, so the exchange alone brings Black little, but Black gets the freer game; White can answer by closing the centre with d5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 O-O 5.e.name: King's Indian Defence: Semi-Classical Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 O-O 5.e.strategy: Develops the bishop and prepares castling in a compact set-up: White holds the centre with a modest pawn structure and waits for Black to declare how the centre will be challenged.

A more active square than e2: the bishop aims at the kingside and backs up a later e4 push. It stands in front of the queen, however, and can be harassed by Black's knights, so White may lose a tempo.

Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop, which then eyes the long diagonal against the g7 bishop, and the pawn also supports c4. White builds a compact structure, but the plan is slow and leaves the king's bishop's job undecided.

The standard waiting move: Black develops a piece and adds a defender to e5, so the e-pawn break can follow with the pawn well backed up. Black keeps a solid position and waits to see how White uses the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 O-O 5.e.name: King's Indian Defence: Semi-Classical Variation, Benoni Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 O-O 5.e.strategy: Prepares a stand in the centre: the pawn covers d5 and b5 and frees the queen's diagonal. It is slow and does nothing for development, and it leaves White free to expand with no concrete counter, so it is a playable but not first-choice setup.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 O-O 5.e.name: King's Indian Defence: Semi-Classical Variation, Hollywood Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 O-O 5.e.strategy: Aims at d4 and prepares ...e5, but the knight can be driven back by d5, so White gains space with tempo. Black develops quickly, but the piece has to move again and the centre is fixed on White's terms.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 O-O 5.g.strategy: Strikes at the c4 pawn at once. As White has chosen the quiet fianchetto set-up, Black meets it by challenging the centre instead of waiting. The game opens and Black's pieces become active against the d4 pawn.

Sets up the standard King's Indian formation: the pawn controls e5 and c5 and prepares the development of the b8 knight, with the g7 bishop waiting for the centre to open. Black chooses the slow, flexible plan against White's quiet fianchetto and keeps every pawn break available.

Challenges d4 from the side at once and opens the g7 bishop's diagonal, a different plan from the standard set-up. Black hopes for an open game and quick queenside play, but White can close the centre with d5 and gain space.

Resolves the tension on White's terms: the exchange removes Black's central pawn and lets White challenge whatever Black puts on d5 with the c3 knight. Black recaptures with a piece and the game stays open, with a fight for the centre squares.

Completes the fianchetto and lets Black take on c4, trusting development to win the pawn back. The bishop eyes the long diagonal and the king gets safe quickly, but White gives up the clearer plan of exchanging on d5 and Black keeps the extra pawn for a while.

Puts the queen behind the c4 pawn, so it can recapture there if Black takes, and after cxd5 it already hits the d5 square. It brings the queen out early, though, and Black can answer with a developing move that gains a tempo, so it is playable but gives White nothing special.

Recaptures with the knight, which stands well centralised, and keeps Black's pawn structure intact. The knight is attacked by the c3 knight, so Black has to decide soon whether to trade, with the g7 bishop already pressing on d4.
A gambit: Black offers a pawn to open lines, but White simply takes on c6 and is a clean pawn up. Open lines for the pieces are not enough compensation here.
Hangs the queen: the c3 knight takes it and Black can only recapture the knight, so the queen is lost for a piece. Recapturing on d5 with the knight keeps the material level.
